newsitem.title: USA: Spring auction season moves in to full swing.
newsitem.headline: Spring auction season moves in to full swing.

text.p: The spring auction season is upon us.
If you're looking for something fun and unusual to do this spring, the big auction houses in New York, and others around the country, are holding a host of sales in May and June.

Auctions can be plenty of fun for the merely curious as well as for collectors. They're a good way to learn about watches, wine, paintings, rock 'n roll mementoes, Judaica -- just about anything you might be interested in collecting.
If you plan to bid at an auction, do your homework beforehand.
Send for the auction house catalogue if one is available. These provide a wealth of information about the items to be sold and about the bidding process.

The items, sold in "lots", are usually on view for a few days before the sale. This is a good time to visit the auction house to learn, ask questions of the experts, and familiarize yourself with things you may want to bid for.

The day of the auction, register. Most sales at major houses are free and open to the public. You may need a credit reference if you want to bid, so bring picture identification with name and address and a major credit card.
To bid at the auction, raise your hand, or a paddle you get when registering. It may be helpful to watch an auction or two before bidding so you become comfortable with the process.

Many houses also accept bids in writing. You can usually pay for your purchase with credit cards or personal checks as well as cash. Some auction houses will store your purchase, if needed, usually for a fee.
And remember that most charge a commission, known as a buyer's premium, generally 10 percent to 15 percent added to the final "hammer" price.
Here's a rundown of some of the things on offer:

Sotheby's in New York is offering manuscripts and printed Americana on May 12, including a four-page letter signed by George Washington from 1780. The presale estimate for the letter, in which the first president protests Congress' treatment of the continental army, is $150,000 to $250,000.

Sotheby's is auctioning tribal art on May 5 and contemporary art on May 6-7. The latter auction is to be benefit the Boston Children's Heart Foundation, with proceeds going to Children's Hospital at Harvard Medical School.
Other auctions at Sotheby's will offer Old Master paintings (May 21), French furniture (May 22), Latin American art (May 29-30) and comic books (June 14).

Christie's is holding a June 25 auction of dresses from the collection of Diana, Princess of Wales. One of the dresses is an ink-blue velvet gown worn to a Reagan White House dinner at which the princess, then still married to Prince Charles, danced with John Travolta.
There are no presale estimates for the dresses; the bidding will start at $5,000 for each, a Christie's spokeswoman said.
Christie's will also offer a selection of autographs on May 14, coins (June 3), books (June 4), American furniture (June 17), stamps (June 20) and watches (June 24).
Another New York auction house, Phillips, will be offering jewelry on May 1 and June 10. It is holding a wine tasting on June 2 and an auction on June 3.

Phillips will also auction a collection of natural history items on June 21; it has offered unusual lots in natural history recently, including fragments of meteorites from Mars at a December auction.
At the end of June, Robert Edwards Auctions will offer more than 750 lots of cards and other baseball items in what it called the largest auction in its 27-year history.
The Hoboken, N.J.-based house, a specialist in baseball memorabilia, will feature the uniform that Lou Gehrig wore when he gave his "Luckiest Man Alive" speech on July 4, 1939.
Bidding for the white-and-blue pinstripe N.Y. Yankee uniform will start at $75,000.
